brief.head: Past 60, more to go
brief.text: Life ex­pectancy at birth in India is about 74, Ajay Shah said, but those who reach 60 or 70 can ex­pect more years still. {065-C04}

brief.head: The test of a state
brief.text: Like win­ning a war, get­ting pen­sions right is a raw test of whether a state can think, Shah said: it needs cal­cu­la­tions over a hun­dred years. {065-C05}

brief.head: Send it abroad
brief.text: Shah’s one re­gret about the NPS: it should have been glob­ally di­ver­si­fied from day one, with per­haps 60 to 80 per cent in­vested abroad. {065-C12}

brief.head: Show your workings
brief.text: The UPS came with no cal­cu­la­tions, Shah said. For OROP, he and Renuka Sane pub­lished all their code and as­sump­tions so any­one could rerun the num­bers. {065-C16}

brief.head: With eyes open
brief.text: The NPS took noth­ing from ex­ist­ing staff, Shah said. Only new re­cruits joined, warned in the job ad­ver­tise­ment: if you don’t like it, don’t join the gov­ern­ment. {065-C10}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s pension promises
lead.head: A wound that will not clot

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 65

body: Amit Varma ar­rived at the shoot with a shav­ing cut that would not stop bleed­ing. With Ajay Shah’s bless­ing he aimed a hairdryer at his lip, and by the time the cam­eras rolled he had a metaphor.
A shal­low cut heals on its own. A body with a thou­sand deep cuts and no way to clot keeps bleed­ing. That, Varma said, made a pretty apt metaphor for the episode’s sub­ject: India’s pen­sions.

Varma first heard of the dan­ger in mid-2023 from the politi­cian Jayaprakash Narayan, who told him it kept him up at night. {065-S02} Varma had never heard of the NPS or the OPS. “No, Amit,” Narayan replied, “we are de­stroy­ing our fu­ture gen­er­a­tion.”

That led him to Shah, one of the ar­chi­tects of the New Pension Scheme. This episode was prompted by its suc­ces­sor, the Unified Pension Scheme, which, Varma said, does things to the NPS that make it just like the OPS.
An econ­o­mist both hosts re­spect, Varma added, has warned that it could lead to the great­est fis­cal dis­as­ter India has seen.
## Promises that grow

Shah’s case rests on one dis­tinc­tion. A de­fined-benefit pen­sion guar­an­tees a pay­out for life, paid in ef­fect by the young to the old. A de­fined-contribution pen­sion makes you save into an ac­count that is yours alone.
“Every sin­gle de­fined ben­e­fit pro­gram in the world has got into trou­ble,” Shah said. {065-C02}

India’s old scheme gave civil ser­vants a 50 per cent de­fined-benefit pen­sion. When Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave put a present value on those prom­ises, the an­swer was 68 per cent of GDP. {065-C06}
## A bi­par­ti­san res­cue

The NDA’s big four, Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee, grasped it at once. Vajpayee signed the file in December 2002, and from January 2004 new cen­tral gov­ern­ment re­cruits joined the NPS in­stead.
What struck Varma was what came next. The UPA gov­ern­ment that fol­lowed re-examined the re­form from scratch and kept it. Manmohan Singh and Chidambaram, he said, got it too.
When the CPI(M) would not back a law, Chidambaram ran the scheme for nine years on pri­vate con­tracts that bound fund man­agers to in­spec­tion and dis­clo­sure. The law came only in 2013.
## How it came un­done
Then, Shah said, the com­mu­nity of thinkers that had made the case for the NPS went home. Flaws went un­fixed, and no­body redid the cal­cu­la­tion of im­plicit pen­sion debt.

Young civil ser­vants who had joined the NPS with their eyes open began de­mand­ing the old scheme. The Congress, Varma noted, pushed it in state after state, though Shah had once briefed Rahul Gandhi on pen­sion re­form.

Varma could not un­der­stand why a small group car­ried such weight when the cost falls on ev­ery­one. Politicians “who should know bet­ter, who do know bet­ter, are ac­tu­ally pan­der­ing to them”, he said.
The UPS, Shah said, tops up any an­nu­ity below 50 per cent from a guar­an­tee fund: in de­riv­a­tives terms a put op­tion, whose cost no­body has pub­lished. {065-C15}

His broader les­son was about re­form it­self. The NPS was struc­tural: your money in your ac­count, noth­ing for politi­cians to fid­dle with. Parametric re­forms leave the old ma­chine and its dials in place. {065-C17}
Varma turned the idea on him­self. A week­end locked away to write, or an oc­ca­sional sprint, is a para­met­ric fix; daily habits are struc­tural.
“We talk here about re­form­ing the state,” he said. “I tell the reader, re­form thy­self.”

second.label: The 2004 handover
second.head: Saved by a market crash
second.deck: How a stock market panic in May 2004 helped keep pension reform alive
body: In the 2004 cam­paign, a Congress can­di­date in Delhi tried to stir anger over lost de­fined-benefit pen­sions. It got no trac­tion, Ajay Shah said.

Then, on 17 May 2004, the stock mar­ket crashed after some CPM politi­cians talked of tear­ing the house down. Shah makes a causal claim: the cri­sis helped Sonia Gandhi set­tle on Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram, Montek Ahluwalia and C Rangarajan as her eco­nomic team. {065-S07}

These were, Shah said, the peo­ple who had been lead­ing the re­forms all along, and the mar­ket quickly lost its jit­ters. The new UPA gov­ern­ment re-examined the NPS from scratch. Shah spent half a day walk­ing Rahul Gandhi and young Congress MPs through it, at a ses­sion or­gan­ised by Bibek Debroy. {065-S08}

quote.text: This is the dream team of the peo­ple that had been lead­ing the re­forms all along.

third.head: Twice the bill till 2029

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the generation that pays twice

body: For about a gen­er­a­tion, Ajay Shah said, gov­ern­ments pay twice: the pen­sions of those al­ready re­tired, and the 10 per cent higher salaries that fund the new ac­counts. {065-C11}

“And this was done by de­sign that there will be a tran­si­tion gen­er­a­tion where you will pay twice,” he said. The pay­off was due around 2029, when pay­ments to the older gen­er­a­tion would start sub­sid­ing.

With no re­searchers mod­el­ling the tran­si­tion, politi­cians saw only the extra cost, and some lost their nerve just be­fore the pay­off. On one side, Shah said, were some one lakh, two lakh or­gan­ised young civil ser­vants; on the other, no pub­lic dis­course at all. {#lakh}
Amit Varma added that the 25-year wait ap­plies to state fi­nances: in­di­vid­u­als in a well-run NPS would do much bet­ter than under the OPS.

p2.title: Promises, promises
p2.deck: How pensions grew from a kindness into a menace, how India fixed them, and how the fix is fraying

from1.head: A wound that will not clot

quote.text: There is not one de­fined ben­e­fit pro­gram that has stayed out of trou­ble.

photo.caption: Atal Bihari Vajpayee, former Prime Minister of India

box.title: The report that started it
box.text: The Project Oasis re­port of 2000, from an ex­pert com­mit­tee led by Surendra Dave, set out the de­sign that be­came the NPS: per­sonal ac­counts, eq­ui­ties and index funds bought at auc­tion for razor-thin fees. Ajay Shah sat on the com­mit­tee. {065-R01}

sections.label: How it began
sections.head: From whip-round to time bomb
sections.caption: how pensions became a bloody mess
body: Pensions began as small acts of grace. At one port, Ajay Shah re­called, when workers’ health broke from lug­ging car­tons, the cur­rent work­ers would pool a lit­tle bit of money to give them a pen­sion. {#port}

Because peo­ple died quickly, the ges­ture cost lit­tle. Bismarck, then the leader of Germany, turned it into an af­fair of state. In 1889 he an­nounced a pen­sion of 50 per cent of the last year’s in­come, paid from age 70, at a time when there were no an­tibi­otics and doc­tors still used leeches.
“So once again, this was a tiny ges­ture which feels nice but was not eco­nom­i­cally ma­te­rial,” Shah said. {065-S03}
## Three forces

Over the fol­low­ing cen­tury the same idea be­came, in Shah’s words, a bloody mess. People lived longer, so life­long pay­ments were worth more. Birth rates col­lapsed, so fewer young peo­ple paid for more old ones. And demo­cratic pol­i­tics kept chip­ping away at the terms: the per­cent­age and the start­ing age.

Here Shah called him­self a one-handed econ­o­mist. Every de­fined-benefit pro­gramme in the world, he said, has re­neged on its prom­ises, or will. {065-C02} Amit Varma ex­plained the phrase: the US President Harry Truman wanted an econ­o­mist who would not keep say­ing “on the other hand”.

~ Varma added that these dan­gers are easy to see with a thirty- or forty-year view. But politicians’ hori­zons are short, and in India there is al­ways an elec­tion around the cor­ner in some state or other.

quote.text: There is not one de­fined ben­e­fit pro­gram that has stayed out of trou­ble.

sections.label: Chalk and cheese
sections.head: Three rooms that look alike
sections.caption: nominal, inflation- and wage-indexed pensions
body: Ajay Shah began with terms. A nom­i­nal pen­sion pays a fixed sum, say Rs 50 on a wage of Rs 100, for the rest of your life. With wise fi­nan­cial plan­ning it can be achieved.

Index it to in­fla­tion and the cost roughly dou­bles, Shah said. Index it to the wages of today’s work­ers and it be­comes as­tro­nom­i­cally ex­pen­sive. “There does not exist a wise man­age­ment strat­egy through which wage in­dex­a­tion can be ob­tained,” he said. {065-C03}

They sound alike, he warned, but they are chalk and cheese. The fair-sounding de­mand be­hind one rank, one pen­sion, that a gen­eral re­tired twenty years ago should get what a new one gets, blows up the num­bers.
## Yours, not ours

Against all of this Shah set the de­fined-contribution pen­sion. The state uses its power only to make you save into your own ac­count. Nobody pays for any­one else, and no­body else can get their claws on your money. {065-C01}
Defined ben­e­fits, he said, pit the young against the old: every Marxist dream of class war­fare.

~ Amit Varma put it in terms of a com­pany. An em­ployer that over­promises pen­sions goes out of busi­ness. The state, spend­ing other people’s money on other peo­ple, as in Milton Friedman’s ma­trix, faces no such check.

quote.text: The beauty of a de­fined con­tri­bu­tion ap­proach is there is no so­cial­i­sa­tion, which is the root of all evil.

sections.label: The old scheme
sections.head: Sixty-eight per cent of GDP
sections.caption: the 68 per cent bombshell
body: The Old Pension Scheme paid civil ser­vants a 50 per cent de­fined-benefit pen­sion. Civil ser­vants are a tiny frac­tion of Indians, and for years no­body no­ticed. Then pay­outs in the rail­ways, the mil­i­tary and the civil ser­vice began to surge, and by the 1990s, Ajay Shah said, sim­ple ex­trap­o­la­tions showed the coun­try could not af­ford them.

In 1998, under the Vajpayee gov­ern­ment, Anand Bordia, a joint sec­re­tary in Maneka Gandhi’s Ministry of Social Justice, worked with Gautam Bhardwaj to set up Project Oasis. It was led by Surendra Dave, found­ing chair­man of SEBI. Shah sat on its ex­pert com­mit­tee.
Dave’s in­tu­ition was that eq­uity re­turns, mod­ern tech­nol­ogy and index funds bought by auc­tion could make a cheap, at­trac­tive pen­sion sys­tem.
## The stock, not the flow

Bhardwaj and Dave then put a present value on the prom­ises made to civil ser­vants: 68 per cent of GDP. {065-S04} Until then peo­ple had watched the flow of pay­ments, dou­bling every six years, with­out see­ing the stock. {065-C06}
The num­ber reached Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee, the big four of the NDA cab­i­net, and all of them got it.
~ Shah drew a line to de­fence. A mighty mil­i­tary is made out of eco­nom­ics, he said, and the first item on the agenda of mil­i­tary re­form is to solve the pen­sions mess. {#military}

quote.text: That was an eye opener and it helped wake up ev­ery­body on the scale of this prob­lem.

sections.label: The new scheme
sections.head: Bought, not sold
sections.caption: how the NPS was designed
body: The NPS, Ajay Shah said, asks the state to make a civil ser­vant do what a so­phis­ti­cated saver would do any­way: save, hold eq­ui­ties, use index funds and keep fees low. {065-C07}

Twenty per cent of pay went into a per­sonal ac­count. The money was run by a small pool of fund man­agers, six in the orig­i­nal in­tent, cho­sen by pub­lic ten­der and run­ning index funds. The only test of an index fund, Shah said, is how lit­tle it charges.
Index funds were po­lit­i­cally safe too: no­body could de­mand a CBI in­ves­ti­ga­tion into why a fund man­ager did badly.
## No sales­men

Shah called one say­ing in fi­nance deeply toxic: that fund man­age­ment is sold, not bought. {065-C08} It is the world of Shah Rukh Khan in the ad­ver­tise­ments, crazy com­mis­sions and a mil­lion agents nudg­ing friends and fam­ily into tax-saving prod­ucts.

The NPS was to be bought. Fund man­agers would get bulk money with­out even know­ing their customers’ names. An ex­pert com­mit­tee would set the de­fault mix of eq­ui­ties, cor­po­rate bonds and gov­ern­ment bonds, and any­one could over­ride it on­line.
~ And every month, Shah said, mem­bers get an SMS telling them what they now own, a num­ber that re­morse­lessly goes up. {#sms}

quote.text: There’s a phrase in fi­nance which is a deeply toxic one which says that fund man­age­ment is sold, not bought.

sections.label: What went wrong
sections.head: The reformers went home
sections.caption: the pension community that disbanded
body: From 1998 to 2004, Ajay Shah said, India had a real pen­sion re­form com­mu­nity: re­search pa­pers, sem­i­nars, op-eds, an in­tel­lec­tual fer­ment. Then the de­ci­sions were taken, ev­ery­one thought the job was done, and the com­mu­nity dis­banded. {065-S12}
“And with­out the ecosys­tem, you’re noth­ing,” Shah said.

Small flaws in the NPS went un­fixed. Equity ex­po­sure stayed timid, a fail­ure of nerve by the civil ser­vants in charge. Military pen­sions drifted into OROP. Pension work moved from KP Krishnan’s DEA to the DFS, and in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory went with it.
## Who pays, who shouts

When young civil ser­vants began de­mand­ing the OPS, there was no­body left to argue back. Karnataka once in­for­mally asked Shah to spend a day with its trade unions; he did, and calls it a mat­ter of talk­ing, en­gag­ing and show­ing cal­cu­la­tions. {#karnataka}

States that go back to the OPS can­not touch the NPS money, which is the workers’ pri­vate prop­erty. Last he heard, Shah said drily, it was not yet easy for Indian gov­ern­ments to ex­pro­pri­ate it. {065-J13}
~ Amit Varma drew the moral: pass­ing a pol­icy is not the end of the story. Quoting what he called Jefferson’s al­leged phrase, he said eter­nal vig­i­lance is still re­quired. {065-J15}

quote.text: Now, in hind­sight, the big­gest tragedy was that that com­mu­nity dis­banded.

sections.label: The new storm
sections.head: A guarantee nobody priced
sections.caption: the Unified Pension Scheme and its put option
body: A storm broke over the out­door shoot. When the hosts re­turned, Amit Varma said the UPS was one of those storms that would not pass eas­ily.

The Unified Pension Scheme keeps a fund, Ajay Shah said, but prom­ises that if a retiree’s an­nu­ity falls below 50 per cent, a guar­an­tee fund will fill the gap. In the lan­guage of de­riv­a­tives, that is a put op­tion on the port­fo­lio, and put op­tions can be pretty ex­pen­sive. {065-C15}

Nobody has pub­lished the cal­cu­la­tions. Pension prom­ises can run to 50 or 100 per cent of GDP, Shah said; in the United States the im­plicit pen­sion debt is 200 per cent. {#usdebt} Without the num­bers, the guar­an­tee could be­come a con­tin­gent li­a­bil­ity dan­gling over the Indian state.
## No dials to twid­dle

The NPS mat­tered, Shah ar­gued, be­cause it was a struc­tural re­form: your own money in your own ac­count, with no fudge fac­tors. Parametric re­forms keep the old ma­chine and leave dials for pol­i­tics to twid­dle. {065-C17}
NREGS, he said, was promised to be self-liquidating: as in­comes rose, no­body would want to work for 100 ru­pees a day. {#nregs} Instead its daily pay­ment kept going up.

~ He feared the same creep in any gov­ern­ment-run uni­ver­sal health­care sys­tem, and bor­rowed a line from Bruce Springsteen for India’s miss­ing thinkers: “Well man, the poets around here don’t write noth­ing at all.” {065-J17}

quote.text: In para­met­ric re­forms, we hold a basic ed­i­fice in­tact and twid­dle with some dials.
The point, how­ever, is to change the Overton win­dow, is to le­git­imize the com­plex re­forms that are needed in the coun­try that are be­yond the hori­zon of an av­er­age pol­i­cy­maker.

p3.title: Inside the room
p3.deck: Cabinet meetings, insurance chiefs, a bleeding lip and a minister’s candour

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how the NDA cabinet signed up for reform
stories.head: Eyes closed, mind made up
body: Ajay Shah worked di­rectly with Yashwant Sinha, S Narayan and UK Sinha, and de­scribes a younger, less po­lite ver­sion of him­self talk­ing fire and brim­stone about what would hap­pen if India did not fix the prob­lem.

They car­ried the case up to Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee. Shah, then in the Ministry of Finance, re­calls the prime min­is­ter send­ing back vari­a­tion after vari­a­tion: sup­pose you do it like this, show me the cal­cu­la­tions. {065-S05}

Vajpayee fi­nally set­tled on what Shah calls “ten, ten and ninety”: a 10 per cent wage hike, so that 100 be­came 110, and a de­duc­tion of 20 into a per­sonal pen­sion ac­count, leav­ing 90. It was, Shah said, pure po­lit­i­cal judge­ment of what was fair.
Shah was not in the de­ci­sive cab­i­net meet­ing. UK Sinha was, and told him the story. The big four favoured the re­form; many other min­is­ters did not.

Vajpayee, Shah said, “had a way of ei­ther ap­pear­ing to be asleep or ac­tu­ally being asleep in meet­ings”. {065-J09} That day he sat with his eyes al­most closed, tak­ing in the de­bate. At the end he ruled: “Yeh to karna hi hai.” This sim­ply has to be done. {065-S06}
He signed the file on 12 December 2002. {#signature} From 1 January 2004, every new cen­tral gov­ern­ment em­ployee went into the new sys­tem.
~ Shah of­fers Vajpayee’s line as a slo­gan for every dreamer, every re­former, every do-gooder: you have to bite the bul­let, and you have to do these things.
stories.why: A re­form that pays off over decades needs a leader will­ing to spend po­lit­i­cal cap­i­tal on gains no voter today will see. Vajpayee asked for the num­bers, judged what was fair, and then de­cided.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma pic­tured a web-series scene of Vajpayee gaz­ing at a young Shah. Shah de­flated it: he never sat with Vajpayee on this ques­tion. {065-J08}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the decisive cabinet meeting

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the day the insurance lobby lost
stories.head: Fourteen chiefs, one reply
body: The in­sur­ance in­dus­try wanted pen­sions for it­self. “We don’t want no stink­ing pen­sion fund man­agers, we don’t want no stink­ing index funds,” was how Ajay Shah put its case. {065-J10}

Chidambaram called a meet­ing with four­teen in­sur­ance CEOs, Surendra Dave be­side him. Shah could at­tend but must not speak. Each CEO said they knew the busi­ness, could do index funds and could even offer guar­an­tees.

Then Chidambaram turned to Dave. What fol­lowed, Shah said, was the most mas­terly fif­teen-minute re­but­tal, while his own heart was in his mouth. Nobody said any­thing after it. {065-S09} Later that day word came: the boss has de­cided, we’re doing NPS.

~ Why it mat­tered, Shah said: until re­tire­ment a pen­sion is just fund man­age­ment, your money, in­her­ited by your heirs. Insurance be­longs only at the end, when sav­ings be­come an an­nu­ity. {065-C09}

quote.text: But Dave’s re­sponse was ab­so­lutely mas­terly, and no­body said any­thing.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the fourteen insurance CEOs

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s morning before the shoot
stories.head: The bleeding lip libertarian
body: Amit Varma shaved on the morn­ing of the shoot, mak­ing “some min­i­mal ef­fort” to look pre­sentable. {065-J01} His mind wan­dered, and he cut his lip.

The cut kept bleed­ing. Varma would not can­cel: “I don’t care if I die, but we gotta shoot.” {065-J02} Ajay Shah, wear­ing his sci­en­tific hat, said oxy­gen makes blood clot and told him to stand in front of a fan. Varma asked if a hairdryer would do, and be­came per­haps the first per­son in his­tory to aim one at his lips.
His se­ri­ous thought: a shal­low cut stops bleed­ing, but a body with a thou­sand deep cuts and no clot­ting bleeds on and on. He found it an apt metaphor for the episode’s sub­ject. {065-S01}
~ The other was a label: this na­tion is re­gret­tably too full of bleed­ing-heart lib­er­als, and here was a bleed­ing lip lib­er­tar­ian. {065-J03}

quote.text: But imag­ine a body where you have a thou­sand deep cuts and the mech­a­nism of clot­ting isn’t there

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the bleeding lip

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a lesson from Yashwant Sinha
stories.head: A mere finance minister
body: In 2002 and 2003, Ajay Shah tried to sell in­fla­tion tar­get­ing to the fi­nance min­is­ter, Yashwant Sinha. Sinha said the idea was way too far from con­ven­tional Indian in­tel­lec­tual dis­course.
“Your baradari is not ready for this,” Sinha told him. India’s econ­o­mists, he said, did not un­der­stand mon­e­tary eco­nom­ics, and the larger com­mu­nity would have to shift its po­si­tion first.
Then came the line. “Then who am I? I’m a mere fi­nance min­is­ter. I can only fol­low. I can’t lead.” {065-S11} Inflation tar­get­ing did ar­rive, in 2015.

~ For Shah the moral is a the­ory of change: whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear only pro­duces small changes within what of­fi­cials al­ready ac­cept. The task is to change the Overton win­dow. {065-C14}
stories.why: Even pow­er­ful min­is­ters act within the range of ideas their ex­perts ac­cept. Lasting re­form, Shah ar­gued, needs a broad com­mu­nity that changes what is think­able. Amit Varma counted the years: thir­teen, the long road to change. {065-R15}

quiz.q: When Bismarck announced his pension in 1889, from what age was it paid, and why was it cheap?
quiz.a: From sev­enty; with no an­tibi­otics, few peo­ple lived much be­yond that age.

quiz.q: What did Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave find the civil service pension promises were worth?
quiz.a: 68 per cent of GDP, for a tiny sliver of the pop­u­la­tion.

quiz.q: Under Vajpayee’s “ten, ten and ninety”, what happened to a civil servant’s pay of 100?
quiz.a: It rose to 110; 20 went into a pen­sion ac­count, leav­ing 90.

quiz.q: What did Vajpayee say at the end of the decisive cabinet meeting on pensions?
quiz.a: “Yeh to karna hi hai”: this sim­ply has to be done.

quiz.q: Who answered the fourteen insurance CEOs in Chidambaram’s meeting, and how long did he take?
quiz.a: Surendra Dave, with what Ajay Shah calls a mas­terly fif­teen-minute re­but­tal.

quiz.q: In the language of derivatives, what is the UPS promise to top up annuities?
quiz.a: A put op­tion on the port­fo­lio, and put op­tions can be pretty ex­pen­sive.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 65. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Otto von Bismarck (André Bockmann, public domain); Atal Bihari Vajpayee (Government of India, GODL-India); Manmohan Singh (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); James Clear (James Clear, CC BY-SA 4.0).

shelf.title: The Project Oasis Report (2000)
shelf.creator: Project Oasis expert committee, led by Surendra Dave
shelf.why: It is the found­ing doc­u­ment of Indian pen­sion re­form: de­fined con­tri­bu­tions, in­di­vid­ual ac­counts and cheap index funds.

shelf.title: Towards Estimating India’s Implicit Pension Debt
shelf.creator: Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave
shelf.why: This num­ber woke up the Vajpayee cab­i­net.

shelf.title: Investment Risk in Indian Pension Sector and Role for Pension Guarantees (2003)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It frames pen­sion guar­an­tees as put op­tions on a port­fo­lio, which can be very ex­pen­sive.

shelf.title: What is the cost of one-rank-one-pension? (2015)
shelf.creator: Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Renuka Sane and Ajay put a cost on the OROP scheme that the hosts blame for crowd­ing out mil­i­tary mod­erni­sa­tion, and pub­lished all their code and as­sump­tions so read­ers can rerun the num­bers.

shelf.title: A sustainable and scalable approach in Indian pension reform (2005)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Further read­ing from the pe­riod when the re­form com­mu­nity was ac­tive and mak­ing the case for the NPS de­sign.

shelf.title: In search of inclusion (2015)
shelf.creator: Renuka Sane and Susan Thomas
shelf.why: Further read­ing on pen­sion sys­tems from Renuka Sane, who Amit notes has spent re­cent years work­ing on this field.

shelf.title: Simulating Pension Income Scenarios with penCalc (2018)
shelf.creator: Renuka Sane and William Price
shelf.why: An ex­am­ple of the pen­sion in­come sim­u­la­tion work Ajay says India badly needs more of.

shelf.title: There be dragons: Off-balance-sheet liabilities of the Indian State (2018)
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Companion read­ing to Ajay’s warn­ing that the UPS guar­an­tee may be­come a con­tin­gent li­a­bil­ity hang­ing over the Indian state.

shelf.title: India’s Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
shelf.why: Ajay and Renuka Sane on the old ver­sus new pen­sion scheme: a bi­par­ti­san re­form built by a small in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, and how in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory van­ished once that com­mu­nity dis­persed.

shelf.title: Jayaprakash Narayan Wants to Mend Our Democracy (Episode 334, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
shelf.why: It is where Amit first learned the stakes, and the con­ver­sa­tion that led to this episode.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into the Indian Military (Episode 31, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay, who speaks to rooms full of gen­er­als, on re­form­ing India’s mil­i­tary, start­ing with pen­sions: with­out fix­ing them there is no money for a mod­ern mil­i­tary.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Atomic Habits
shelf.creator: James Clear
shelf.why: The best book on pro­duc­tiv­ity Amit has read, and the one to start with if you read only one: turn your mind from goals to habits and pro­cesses, the com­pound in­ter­est of self-improvement, and use small re­wards to make habits stick.

laughs.text: Amit, bleed­ing and re­fus­ing to can­cel: ‘Man, we gotta shoot. I don’t care if I die, but we gotta shoot.’ And on his blood-streaked torso: ‘Had my torso been a lit­tle more bet­ter de­vel­oped, it would have been an ex­cep­tion­ally en­tic­ing scene, but it wasn’t. It was just bloody.’
Amit: ‘Just as this na­tion is re­gret­tably too full of bleed­ing heart lib­er­als, here you had a bleed­ing lip lib­er­tar­ian. Though I do not like la­bels, Pushpa, so we shall not go there.’

Amit on wage-indexed pen­sions: ‘After I re­tire, I want the state to give me every month half of BeerBiceps’ in­come. And we’ll be fine. That’s where I want it in­dexed... As far as money is con­cerned, I’m not doing his con­tent.’
Ajay on the night­mare head­line gov­ern­ments fear: ‘Oh, this per­son was a sec­re­tary to gov­ern­ment and now she’s sit­ting by the gates of the Bangalore Metro beg­ging for a free idli sam­bar.’
Ajay on Vajpayee in meet­ings: ‘he had a way of ei­ther ap­pear­ing to be asleep or ac­tu­ally being asleep in meet­ings. Okay, and you could never tell, but he was a wise man.’
Ajay chan­nelling the in­sur­ance lobby: ‘We don’t want no stink­ing pen­sion fund man­agers, we don’t want no stink­ing index funds.’

After Ajay is told to keep quiet in the in­sur­ance CEOs’ meet­ing, Amit: ‘Gentle reader, this per­son here who looks like an elder states­man was once a fire­brand rev­o­lu­tion­ary, right? You haven’t seen that side of him.’

Ajay’s dry aside on states try­ing to grab NPS money: ‘last I heard it was not yet easy for gov­ern­ments in India to ex­pro­pri­ate our pri­vate prop­erty. I mean I know they can do it, but it is still hard.’

Harry Truman’s plea for a ‘one-handed economist’, one who wouldn’t keep say­ing ‘on the other hand’. Ajay calls him­self one on de­fined-benefit pen­sions, and Amit ex­plains why that cer­tainty is rare.
Ajay in­verts Mark Antony’s line from Julius Caesar, 26 years after Project Oasis: ‘I come to praise the NPS, not bury it.’
Ajay quotes Bruce Springsteen on India’s miss­ing pol­icy in­tel­lec­tu­als: ‘Well man, the poets around here don’t write noth­ing at all. They just stand by and let it all be.’
Amit quotes Annie Dillard, ‘How we spend our days is how we spend our lives’, to argue for struc­tural re­form through daily habits rather than oc­ca­sional sprints.
